header: Abdul Khaliq vs Wasi-ud-Din Khattak & another
For Petitioner(s): Syed Naveed Ali Shah, Advocate.
For Respondent No.2: Mr. Muhammad Zia-Ullah, Advocate.
J U D G M E N T
body: FARAH JAMSHED, J.- Impugned herein are the judgments and orders dated 29.01.2018, passed in civil appeal No.32/13 of 2012, rendered by the learned Additional District & Sessions Judge-I, Peshawar and order dated 15.09.2020, passed in review petition bearing No.03/Review by the learned Additional District Judge-X, Peshawar, whereby, the appeal as well as review petition filed by the petitioner, were dismissed.

02. The chequered history of this civil revision petition is that the petitioner/plaintiff (Abdul Khaliq) filed a suit against the respondents/defendants, for specific performance and possession based on a registered deed No.4675 dated 27/11/1999 with respect to land measuring 03-Kanal in Khasra No.54 Khatta No.416/496, situated in the revenue estate of Moza Bhana Mari, District Peshawar. He also prayed for a decree for possession, recovery, and compensation as per the agreement deed dated 14/07/2001, as well as permanent injunction.

03. On service of summons, the respondents/defendants put their appearance before the learned trial court and submitted their written statement, raising therein, legal and factual objections. The learned trial court, after framing of issues, recording of evidence, and hearing arguments of the learned counsel for the parties, dismissed the suit of the petitioner vide its judgment dated 16.07.2012.

04. Being aggrieved, the petitioner filed an appeal bearing No.32/13, which was dismissed by the learned appellate court vide judgment and order dated 29.01.2018. Feeling unhappy, the petitioner filed review petition under section 114 read with section 7 of CPC for reviewing the said judgment and order dated 29.01.2018 and reversing the findings of the learned appellate court. The learned court, after hearing arguments, dismissed the review petition vide order dated 15.09.2020. Hence, this civil revision petition.
05. Arguments heard and record perused.

06. Perusal of the record indicates that a suit bearing No.149/1 was instituted by the petitioner for specific performance and possession on the basis of an agreement deed No.4675 executed on 27.11.1999 with respect to the land measuring 03-Kanal, as already mentioned earlier.

07. The record further indicates that another suit bearing No.70/1 neem was filed by respondent No.1 & another against the present petitioner & others, for the grant of decree in the following terms: - (A) i. recovery of Rs.18,00,000/- (balance consideration price of property, fully described in the same agreements dated 27.11.1999, 14.07.2001, 20.09.2001 & 22.09.2001) and ii. Rs.50,00,000/- as special damages on account of mental torture, physical trouble, defamation and financial loss and breach of contract.
(B) i. forfeiture and confiscation to the plaintiffs of Rs.4,00,000/- according to agreement dated 14.07.2001.
ii. Award of special compensatory cost under section 35-A CPC, and iii. cancellation of agreement dated 27.11.1999 and registered deeds No.407 to 410 dated 26.01.2002, in alternative.

08. The said suit was initially decreed exparte vide order dated 14.12.2012, however, later vide order dated 05.03.2013, the exparte order was set aside. On 02.04.2013, the plaintiff submitted an application for sine die adjournment, till the final disposal of pending appeal before this court against the order dated 16.07.2012 of the learned Civil Judge-XXX, Peshawar. The said application was accepted, and the case was adjourned sine die vide order dated 02.04.2013.

09. It is evident from the record that both the aforementioned suits were instituted on the basis of the same agreement between the parties. However, suit bearing No.149/1 was decided on merits while the other suit bearing No.70/1 neem, remained pending and later adjourned sine die. The courts below appear to have proceeded on an incorrect conception that the latter suit bearing No.70/1 neem, was decreed on 14.12.2012, whereas, in fact the said suit was initially decreed ex-parte, but, later on, on the application of the plaintiff, the ex-parte decree and order was set aside vide order dated 05.03.2013 and the original suit was restored with costs. It is manifest from the record that both the learned courts below fell into a patent error in presuming that the said suit had attained finality by way of decree dated 14.12.2012, whereas, in actuality, the decree in question was an ex-parte, which was subsequently set aside through a lawful order dated 05.03.2013, restoring the suit to its original position. Thereafter, the matter was not finally adjudicated but was only adjourned sine die, and thus continued to remain pending for determination. In such circumstances, treating the suit as finally decreed was a clear misreading and non-reading of the record, rendering the impugned findings legally unsustainable. This material aspect has escaped the attention of the learned appellate court while deciding appeal No.32/13 on 29.01.2018 and later while dismissing Review Petition No.3 vide order dated 15.09.2020. Such non-consideration of a vital point has resulted in miscarriage of justice, as the interconnected nature of both proceedings, arising out of the same agreement, required proper appreciation and concurrent adjudication. Consequently, the impugned judgments and orders cannot be sustained, and the matter warrants remand for a fresh decision after proper consideration of all relevant aspects.

10. As regards the preliminary objection of the petition being time-barred, the same is hereby brushed aside in the peculiar circumstances of the case. There can be no dispute that a truly void order, being a nullity in the eye of law, may not attract the ordinary bar of limitation. At the same time, it is equally settled that not every illegal or erroneous order does becomes void automatically. The question, therefore, is whether the impugned judgment is merely an erroneous exercise of jurisdiction, or a nullity that must be ignored altogether.

11. The distinction is recognized in our jurisprudence. In Muhammad Swaleh case, the Supreme Court explained that where a court assumes jurisdiction not vested in it by law, or fails to exercise its jurisdiction, the resulting order is void. However, if the court acts illegally or with material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction, the order is voidable. The apex Court observed that expressions like “void order” and “order without jurisdiction” are often overworked and must be used with caution, because an order does not cease to exist merely because of those labels.

12. The same principle was reiterated by the Supreme Court when it explicitly held that the bar of limitation does not operate in respect of void orders; it applies to erroneous orders. An order that is truly without jurisdiction and void need not even be formally set aside. Conversely, where the court had jurisdiction but committed a legal error in the exercise thereof, the order remains challengeable according to law and within limitation.

13. Tested on the above touchstone, the impugned appellate’s court judgment dated 29.1.2018 is not a void order. The appellate court certainly had jurisdiction to hear Muhammad Swaleh and another vs. Messrs United Grain and Fodder Agencies (PLD 1964 SC 97)
Messrs Conforce Ltd vs. Syed Ali Shah etc (PLD 1977 SC 599) Land Acquisition Collector, Nowshera & others vs. Sarfaraz Khan & others (PLD 2001 SC 514)

the appeal; its error was in misinterpreting the legal effect of the setting aside of the ex parte decree and the consequent restoration, followed by sine die adjournment, of the connected suit. This error was significant and went to the correctness of the decision, but it did not strip the appellate court of jurisdiction nor render the order void. Thus, the argument that no limitation runs against a void order does not, by itself, resolve the issue of delay in the present case.

14. Be that as it may, the revisional interference is still warranted on merits, because the appellate court proceeded on an incorrect assumption that the ex parte decree in the connected suit continued to subsist. Once that decree had been set aside, it ceased to exist and lost its operative effect. The restored suit still pending notwithstanding its sine die adjournment, and the controversy arising out of the same agreement deed dated 27.11.1999 could not be resolved by treating one proceeding as final and the other as barred by a decree which no longer exist. The correct and proper course was to consider both matters together, so as to avoid conflicting findings and ensuring an effective adjudication of the real dispute.

15. The apprehension that adjudication of the restored suit on its own merits may prejudice the earlier decision is misconceived. Once the exparte decree was set aside, the restored suit was legally reinitiated and had to be decided independently on the basis of evidence and law. Any notion of finality attached to the initial exparte decree stood is nullified by its setting aside, and no prejudice can arise from a lawfully revived proceeding. The trial court, while deciding both suits together, shall ensure that neither party is allowed to derive an unfair advantage from any procedural overlap, and that the controversy is determined strictly on merits, without influenced by earlier non-existent exparte decree.

16. In this view of the matter, the impugned judgment cannot be sustained. The revision petition is accordingly accepted. The impugned judgment of the appellate court is set aside, and the case is remanded to the trial court with the direction to take up both suits together and decide them in accordance with law, after affording fair opportunity to the parties.
17. The parties are directed to appear before the learned trial court on 09.04.2026.
